title: The hidden cost of the quick question

audience.who: knowledge workers and the managers of corporate teams, on chat and email all day
audience.knows: what being interrupted feels like and that focus is hard to hold; probably no model of why a short interruption costs more than its length
audience.cares_about: getting their own deep work done without becoming the colleague who never answers

outcome: Before sending or answering the next quick question, the viewer can tell whether it needs an answer now, and can propose to their team two or three concrete habits that batch questions and protect blocks of focused time
through_line: A quick question is never only the minute it takes to answer: every switch also costs the time and attention it takes to get back into the work, so a team protects focus by choosing when questions land, not by asking fewer of them

arc_plan.what: One ordinary moment: someone deep in a piece of work gets a one-line message asking something that takes a minute to answer; the question we pose is where the rest of the cost goes. Framed as invented and typical, no named company

Name the two parts of an interruption's cost: the visible part (answering) and the hidden part (switching away and finding the thread again), using only the terms the knowledge sheet establishes, such as task switching and attention residue

The mechanism shown running on the same piece of work: the thread is held, dropped for the question, and picked back up with a re-entry cost each time; then the same morning repeated with several quick questions, so the hidden part visibly piles up while the visible part stays small. Any magnitude is either from the knowledge sheet with its caveat or explicitly hypothetical
Scale it from one person to a team: each person's quick question is cheap to send and the cost lands on someone else's focus; the asker is not careless, the system makes now the default
Two or three team habits that change when questions land, not whether they are asked, each one tied back to the re-entry cost it removes; close on the opening moment handled differently

must_cover.what: the cost of an interruption is more than the time spent answering it: there is a switching and getting-back-in cost
what task switching and attention residue are, stated only as the knowledge sheet supports them
any figure about recovery time or switching cost, only if the knowledge sheet establishes it with its caveat; otherwise the size is shown in clearly hypothetical framing
the cost accumulates over a day of several small interruptions, shown as objects that pile up
a close of two or three practical team habits, such as batching questions or agreed focus blocks, worded as the knowledge sheet supports
asking questions is still good: the lesson changes when and how, not whether

must_avoid: any number not established and caveated in the knowledge sheet, including widely repeated recovery-time figures repeated as fact
multitasking myths stated as settled science
blaming the person who asks, or telling viewers to stop asking questions
a productivity-guru or teacherly tone, or telling the viewer they have been doing it wrong
naming or criticising real chat or email products
a list of tips that is not tied back to the mechanism
a cartoony register: mascots, bouncy motion, glow
example_posture: One invented, ordinary office worker on one piece of focused work (say, a report or a plan) on one morning, framed as typical, not as a case study; the questions are plausible one-liners from colleagues; no real company, no industry jargon, no villain.
visual_direction: Magazine-like and editorial: generous paper space, strong type, one idea per spread. The cost shown as data you can count: a grid of time units stamped as they are lost, a pile of small interruptions that grows across the morning, the one piece of work held in a slot that is swapped out and back. The visible minute and the hidden re-entry cost always sit side by side so the difference is the picture. The same morning layout returns at the payoff with the questions moved to an agreed time.
voice_note: A capable colleague who has been both the interrupter and the interrupted; level, a little dry, never preachy. Say each point once and keep it short; about two and a half minutes means the mechanism gets the time and the habits get one line each.
open_questions: Is there a team or organisation norm on response times or focus time to align with? None was given, so the habits stay generic.
Should the worker be seen as a person or only through their desk, screen and work? The notes did not say; the storyboard decides within the editorial look.

look.note: From the request notes: editorial, magazine-like explainer; data as objects (stamped unit grids, piles, a held slot that swaps); practical close of two or three team habits.
